## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.60705.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.60705.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

Your detailed investigation of the interplay between visual attention and value-based choice from the broader perspective of goal-directed behavior has provided clear findings that challenge popular decision-making models in neuroeconomics – according to which visual attention towards a choice option increases its estimated subjective value. Your finding that visual attention modulates the integration of goal-relevant evidence rather than value, obtained using state-of-the-art cognitive modeling, is relevant to a broad research community spanning across cognitive psychology and neuroeconomics. Congratulations for an insightful article.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Visual attention modulates the integration of goal-relevant evidence and not value" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Christian Büchel as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Alexandre L S Filipowicz (Reviewer #2); Sebastian Gluth (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

This manuscript describes a behavioral modeling study which aims at challenging popular decision-making models in neuroeconomics – including the “attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM)” – according to which attention towards a choice option increases its estimated subjective value (and thus its probability of being chosen). By asking participants to either choose their most preferred option (“like” frame) but also their least preferred option (“dislike” frame), the authors report that human subjects are more likely to unselect the option that they fixate more in the “dislike” frame – a finding not predicted by the aDDM. The authors report a similar framing effect in a perceptual decision-making task, and provide a theoretical validation of this framing effect. The research question of the interplay between attention and value-based choice, and the obtained findings, are relevant to a broad research community spanning across cognitive psychology and neuroeconomics. The methodology applied by the authors is sound and the manuscript is well-written.

Despite these merits, one important concern raised by the reviews is that the current manuscript does not provide an accurate description of the literature on this issue. While neuroeconomics does focus on “value” as the quantity being accumulated, existing research does not predict nor claim that “value” is the only quantity to which gaze-contingent effects should apply. Indeed, as raised by reviewer #2, gaze-dependent attention has already been shown to influence evidence accumulation in non-value-based decisions (Tavares et al., 2017), suggesting that this phenomenon is not restricted to value. Furthermore, as raised by reviewer #3, the current study overlaps with (Kovach et al., 2014) which has shown that the influence of attention on choice reverses in a “dislike” frame – something that the authors currently acknowledge only in the Appendix.

Nevertheless, reviewers agree that the aDDM has become dominant in neuroeconomics when it comes to modeling the interplay of attention, valuation and decision making. And so the current study conveys the important and timely message to the neuroeconomics community that attention is not primarily driven by values but by goals. To convey this message accurately, we think that a more balanced description of the existing literature is warranted in the Introduction and Discussion sections (including the work that provides clues toward the findings obtained by the authors). This will not significantly reduce the novelty of the study (which is not the main factor driving our evaluation in any case), but will provide a more accurate picture of the field and thus the key contributions of the study. The main strengths of the current study are the experimental design and the robust cognitive modeling methods which together provide an unambiguous answer to the research question addressed by the authors.

Beyond this first concern regarding the literature/theoretical framing of the study, there are other concerns shared by the reviewers, listed below, that the authors should address in a detailed point-by-point response before considering the manuscript as suitable for publication at eLife.

Main concerns (beyond the first concern raised above):

1) Effect of last fixation on framing effects. After reading the manuscript, it appears possible that the framing effects are entirely driven by the last fixation. That is, the increase in choice probability of the more disliked item might be entirely driven by the fact that the last fixation is usually made on the chosen option. Therefore, it would be important to repeat the analysis and exclude the last fixation to see whether the effects still exist when considering only middle and first fixations. It would also be very interesting to see how the effects develop over time within a trial – i.e., at which fixation number (or time point) the influence of attention on choice is strongest – or at which fixation number (or time point) the probability to fixate on the goal-relevant option is highest.

2) Optimal information acquisition model. The reviewers have found the proof of the optimal information acquisition model in the Appendix extremely hard to follow. Reviewer #3 rightly states that all of this may be fairly standard in econometrics, but eLife is a journal read by many life scientists, including neuroscientists and psychologists. eLife readers will have a very hard time following the proof. It is nice that the main text provides a general intuition of the proof, but the proof in the Appendix should also be amended with some more explanations and intuitions. Notations like μi1 and μi2 and then μi1, 2 (i.e., three different things that have almost exactly the same notation) are not very helpful. Regarding the optimal information acquisition model, there are two recent preprints that make a very similar argument, which is that it is optimal to allocate attention on the most promising choice candidates in the case of multi-alternative decision making: Callaway et al., PsyArXiv; and Jang et al., bioRxiv. These preprints should be cited, since they do not reduce in any way the novelty and appeal of the current study.

3) Effect of accumulation asymmetries on confidence. The authors nicely show that GLAM is only capable of reproducing the influence of sum(Value) / sum(Dots) by assuming the presence of an attention bias. The authors conclude that this indicates that the confidence effect may be "caused by the asymmetries in the accumulation process generated by visual attention". The authors should be more explicit to unpack their reasoning. The reason GLAM (with bias) can account for the confidence effect is the multiplicative interaction of attention and valuation: If there are two high-value items (let's say +10 and +10), then an attention bias of 0.3 leads to accumulation rates of 10 vs. 10*0.3 = 3, so a difference of 7. But if there are two low-value items (e.g., +1 and +1), then the difference is only 0.7. Thus, as soon as there is an imbalance in allocated attention between two options, the difference in accumulation rates between those two options is higher if the options have higher values. This will eventually lead to a larger effect on δ(e).

4) Effect of hunger on value-based decisions. Hunger likely plays an important factor to turn this from a cognitive task to a value-based task. However, other than stating that participants were instructed to fast for four hours, I found no mention of measures used to validate hunger. Is a four hour fasting window enough to make people feel hungry? If so, how was participant hunger measured and/or controlled?

5) Participant drop-out rate. The participant drop-out rate seems extremely high (~20-25%), and seems mainly due to difficulties with how the BDM scale was interpreted. With such a high overall drop-out rate, how can the authors be sure that participant responses on this measure are reliable (even the participants who were included in the analyses)? The authors should discuss explicitly this high drop-out rate.

claims.claim: Middle fixations duration increases when the difference in value ratings of the fixated minus unfixated item increases in like and most frames.
claims.source: Previous studies (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Tavares et al., 2017) have reported that middle fixations duration increases when the difference in value ratings (or perceptual evidence) of the fixated minus unfixated item increases. We replicated this result for our like and most frames but critically the effect was reversed in dislike and fewest frames (i.e. middle fixations durations decreased when the relative value of the fixated item was higher).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claims.claim: The effect on middle fixations duration was reversed in dislike and fewest frames.
claims.source: We replicated this result for our like and most frames but critically the effect was reversed in dislike and fewest frames (i.e. middle fixations durations decreased when the relative value of the fixated item was higher).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: After an initial phase in which there was no clear gaze preference for any of the items, fixations were correlated with the frame-relevant item.
claims.source: We observed that after an initial phase in which there was no clear gaze preference for any of the items (note that given the gaze-contingent design participants must explore both alternatives), fixations were correlated with the frame-relevant item: during like frame, fixations positions were positively correlated with ΔValue, that is the fixations were directed towards the item with higher value; during dislike frame the behaviour was the opposite: fixations were negatively correlated with ΔValue, indicating a preference for the option with lower value.
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-series analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The magnitude of ΔValue (|ΔValue|) had a positive influence on confidence in like and dislike frames.
claims.source: We found that the magnitude of ΔValue (|ΔValue|) had a positive influence on confidence in like (z = 5.465, p<0.001) and dislike (z = 6.300, p<0.001) frames, indicating that participants reported higher confidence when the items have a larger difference in value; this effect was larger in the dislike frame (t(30) = -4.72, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Reaction time (RT) had a negative effect on confidence in like and dislike frames.
claims.source: Reaction time (RT) had a negative effect on confidence in like (z = −6.373, p<0.001) and dislike (z = −7.739, p<0.001) frames, that is, confidence was lower when the RTs were longer.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Higher number of gaze switches (gaze shift frequency, GSF) predicted lower values of confidence in like and dislike frames.
claims.source: Additionally, we found that, in both conditions, higher number of gaze switches (i.e. gaze shift frequency, GSF) predicted lower values of confidence in like (z = −2.365, p<0.05) and dislike (z = −2.589, p<0.05) frames, as reported in Folke et al., 2017.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: ΣValue had a positive effect on confidence in the like frame.
claims.source: As in Folke et al., 2017, we found a positive effect of ΣValue on confidence in the like frame (z = 3.206, p<0.01); that is, participants reported a higher confidence level when both options were high in value.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The effect of ΣValue on confidence was inverted in the dislike frame.
claims.source: Interestingly, this effect was inverted in the dislike frame (z = −4.492, p<0.001), with a significant difference between the two frames (t(30)=9.91, p<0.001) This means that, contrary to what happened in the like frame in which confidence was boosted when both items had high value, in the dislike frame confidence increased when both items had low value.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: The change in context generates a reassessment of the evidence used to generate the confidence reports.
claims.source: This novel finding reveals that the change in context also generates a reassessment of the evidence used to generate the confidence reports; that is, confidence also tracks goal-relevant information.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about confidence.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, |ΔDots| had a positive influence on confidence in most and fewest frames.
claims.source: Specifically, we found that |ΔDots| had a positive influence on confidence in most (z = 3.546, p<0.001) and fewest frames (z = 7.571, p<0.001), indicating that participants reported higher confidence when the evidence was stronger.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: The effect of absolute evidence |ΔDots| on confidence was bigger in the fewest frame.
claims.source: The effect of absolute evidence |ΔDots| on confidence was bigger in the fewest frame (t(31)=-4.716, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, RT had a negative effect over confidence in most and fewest frames.
claims.source: RT had a negative effect over confidence in most (z = −7.599, p<0.001) and fewest frames (z = −5.51, p<0.001), that is, faster trials were associated with higher confidence.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, GSF predicted lower values of confidence in most and fewest frames.
claims.source: We also found that GSF predicted lower values of confidence in most (z = −4.354, p<0.001) and fewest (z = −5.204, p<0.001) frames.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the effect of the sum of evidence (ΣDots) on confidence changes sign depending on the frame.
claims.source: Critically (like in the Value Experiment), the effect of the sum of evidence (ΣDots) on confidence also changes sign depending on the frame. While ΣDots had a positive effect over confidence in the most frame (z = 2.061, p<0.05), this effect is the opposite in the fewest frame (z = −7.135, p<0.001), with a significant difference between the parameters in both frames (t(31)=14.621, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: The GLAM belongs to the family of race models and approximates the aDDM model.
claims.source: The GLAM belongs to the family of race models and approximates the aDDM model (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011) in which the dynamic aspect is discarded, favouring a more efficient estimation of the parameters.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claims.claim: The GLAM allows testing the prediction of the confidence measures as balance of evidence.
claims.source: This model was chosen since, unlike the aDDM, it allowed us to test the prediction of the confidence measures as balance of evidence (Vickers, 1979; Kepecs et al., 2008; De Martino et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing GLAM over aDDM.

claims.claim: In both experiments, goal-relevant evidence (not the value or the number of dots) was used to fit the models in the dislike and fewest frames.
claims.source: Crucially, in both experiments, we used goal-relevant evidence (not the value or the number of dots) to fit the models in the dislike and fewest frames (for further details see the Materials and methods Attentional Model: Glam section).
claims.evidence: This describes a key methodological choice in the modeling approach.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, the model replicated the observed decrease of RT when |ΔValue| is high.
claims.source: In both like and dislike frames, the model replicated the observed decrease of RT when |ΔValue| is high, that is, the increase in speed of response in easier trials (bigger value difference).
claims.evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, the RT simulated by the models significantly correlated with the RT values observed in participants odd-numbered trials.
claims.source: The RT simulated by the models significantly correlated with the RT values observed in participants odd-numbered trials (Like: r(29)=0.90, p<0.001; Dislike: r(29)=0.89, p<0.001) (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, the model correctly predicted a higher probability of choosing the right item when ΔValue is higher in the like frame.
claims.source: In the like frame, the model also correctly predicted a higher probability of choosing the right item when ΔValue is higher.
claims.evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, in the dislike frame, the model captured the change in the task goal and predicted that the selection of the right item will occur when -ΔValue is higher.
claims.source: In the dislike frame, the model captured the change in the task goal and predicted that the selection of the right item will occur when -ΔValue is higher, that is when the value of the left item is higher.
claims.evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, the observed and predicted probabilities of choosing the most valuable item were significantly correlated in both frames.
claims.source: Overall, in both frames the observed and predicted probabilities of choosing the most valuable item were significantly correlated (Like: r(29)=0.80, p<0.001; Dislike: r(29)=0.79, p<0.001) (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, the models predicted choice depending on the difference in gaze (ΔGaze) in both frames.
claims.source: In both frames, the models also predicted choice depending on the difference in gaze (ΔGaze = gright – gleft), that is, that the probability of choosing the right item increases when the time spent observing that item is higher.
claims.evidence: This is supported by model simulations.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, most of the participants had a positive gaze influence and it was properly predicted by the model in both frames.
claims.source: As in Thomas et al., 2019, most of the participants had a positive gaze influence and it was properly predicted by the model in both frames (Like: r(29)=0.68, p<0.001; Dislike: r(29)=0.63, p<0.001) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the model simulations replicated the relationship between RT and |ΔDots|.
claims.source: We replicated the relationship between RT and |ΔDots| (Most: r(26)=0.97, p<0.001; Fewest: r(26)=0.98, p<0.001) (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the model predicted a higher probability of choosing the right-hand item when ΔDots is higher in the most frame and when -ΔDots is higher in the fewest frame.
claims.source: As in the value-based experiment, the model also predicted a higher probability of choosing the right-hand item when ΔDots is higher in the most frame and when -ΔDots is higher in the fewest frame.
claims.evidence: This is supported by model simulations compared to experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the simulated choices only in the fewest frame were significantly correlated with the observed data.
claims.source: However, in the Perceptual Experiment, the simulated choices only in the fewest frame were significantly correlated with the observed data, although we observed a non-significant trend in the most frame (Most: r(26)=0.69, p<0.001; Fewest: r(26)=0.37, p=0.051) (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the model predicted that choice was linked to ΔGaze in both frames.
claims.source: In both frames, we observed that the model predicted that choice was linked to ΔGaze and, as in the Value Experiment, we show that the gaze influence predicted by the model is indeed observed in the data (Most: r(26)=0.65, p<0.001; Fewest: r(26)=0.47, p<0.05) (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing model predictions to data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Models fitted without accounting for the change in goal-relevant evidence provided a poor fit of the data.
claims.source: Results of the models fitted without accounting for the change in goal-relevant evidence provided a poor fit of the data, these results are presented in Appendix 5—figures 1–3 and 6.
claims.evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis presented in the appendix.

claims.claim: For dislike and fewest frames, the best aDDM model was the one fitted using goal-relevant evidence.
claims.source: Additionally, we were able to mirror the results obtained with GLAM using aDDM (Krajbich et al., 2010; Tavares et al., 2017). For dislike and fewest frames, the best model was the one fitted using goal-relevant evidence (see Appendix 7 for details).
claims.evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis presented in the appendix.

claims.claim: Balance of evidence is defined as the absolute difference between the accumulators for each option at the moment of choice.
claims.source: Balance of evidence is defined as the absolute difference between the accumulators for each option at the moment of choice, which is when one of them reaches the decision threshold (i.e., Δe = |Eright(tfinal) - Eleft(tfinal)|) (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This defines a computational measure used in the modeling.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, the model replicated the pattern of results obtained experimentally for confidence.
claims.source: We found that this model replicated the pattern of results we obtained experimentally (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparing model simulations to experimental data.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, ΣValue boosted Δe in the like frame and reduced Δe in the dislike frame.
claims.source: As we have shown when analysing confidence, ΣValue boosted Δe in the like frame (βΣValue = 0.071, t(37196) = 14.21, p<0.001) and reduced Δe in the dislike frame (βΣValue = −0.061, t(37196) = −12.07, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations.

claims.claim: In the Value Experiment, the replication of the effect for ΣValue over Δe with GLAM did not hold when the gaze bias was taken out of the model.
claims.source: Interestingly, the replication of the effect for ΣValue over Δe with GLAM did not hold when the gaze bias was taken out of the model in like (βΣValue = −0.007, t(37196) = −1.495, p=0.13, ns) and dislike (βΣValue = −0.002, t(37196) = −0.413, p=0.679, ns) frames (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, ΣDots boosted Δe in the most frame and reduced Δe in the fewest frame.
claims.source: We found that ΣDots boosted Δe in the most frame (Most : βΣDots = 0.029, t(33596) = 4.71, p<0.001) and reduced Δe in the fewest frame (Fewest : βΣDots = −0.088, t(33596) = −14.41, p<0.001) .
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations.

claims.claim: In the Perceptual Experiment, the effect of ΣDots on Δe disappeared when the gaze bias was taken out of the model.
claims.source: As in the Value Experiment, this effect disappeared when the gaze bias was taken out of the model (Most: βΣDots = −0.0002, t(33596) = −0.04, p=0.96, ns; Fewest: βΣDots = −0.006, t(33596) = −1.03, p=0.29, ns) (see Appendix 8—figure 2 and Appendix 8—figure 3B,E for more details).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model simulations.

claims.claim: The model is capable of capturing the novel empirical effect on confidence identified experimentally.
claims.source: Overall, these results show how the model is capable of capturing the novel empirical effect on confidence we identified experimentally, giving computational support to the hypothesis that goal-relevant evidence is fed to second order processes like confidence.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claims.claim: Asymmetries in the accumulation process, in particular the multiplicative effect of attention over accumulation of evidence, may enhance the differences between items that are more relevant for the frame.
claims.source: It also hints at a potential origin to the effects of the sum of evidence (i.e. ΣValue, ΣDots) on confidence: asymmetries in the accumulation process, in particular the multiplicative effect of attention over accumulation of evidence, may enhance the differences between items that are more relevant for the frame.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference about the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claims.claim: When one has to choose the best item, it is more useful to acquire information that is likely to change the ranking at the top than information that changes the ranking at the bottom.
claims.source: The intuition behind both results is that when one has to choose the best item, it is more useful to acquire information that is likely to change the ranking at the top (i.e. between best or second best item) than information that changes the ranking at the bottom, since these items won't be selected (e.g. 4th and 5th item).
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of the intuition behind the economic model.

claims.claim: The reverse is true when one is tasked to select which item to eliminate.
claims.source: Crucially, the reverse is true when one is tasked to select which item to eliminate.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claims.claim: In many ecological settings, in which there are more than two options, the optimal strategy involves acquiring asymmetric information depending on the goal.
claims.source: Our model suggests that in many ecological settings, in which there are more than two options, the optimal strategy involves acquiring asymmetric information depending on the goal.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claims.claim: It is only when there are only two options that individuals are indifferent about which information to acquire.
claims.source: It is only when there are only two options that individuals are indifferent about which information to acquire.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claims.claim: The results favour the hypothesis that attention is allocated depending on the behavioural goal of the task in both perceptual and value-based tasks.
claims.source: Our results favour the second hypothesis: specifically, we show that, in both perceptual and value-based tasks, attention is allocated depending on the behavioural goal of the task.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claims.claim: The findings speak in favour of a more general role played by attention in prioritising the information needed to fulfil a behavioural goal in both value and perceptual choices.
claims.source: Our findings speak in favour of a more general role played by attention in prioritising the information needed to fulfil a behavioural goal in both value and perceptual choices (Gottlieb, 2012; Kovach et al., 2014; Glickman et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by citations to related work.

claims.claim: The seeking of goal-relevant information is observed along the trial, opposing the assumption that attentional sampling is random except for the last fixation.
claims.source: Importantly, the seeking of goal-relevant information is observed along the trial, opposing the assumption that attentional sampling is random except for the last fixation (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; see Gluth et al., 2018; Gluth et al., 2020 for additional support for this idea).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by citations.

claims.claim: The fact that almost identical results were found in a follow-up perceptual study suggests that attention acts on a more fundamental mechanism of information processing that goes beyond simple Pavlovian influences.
claims.source: However, the fact that we found almost identical results in a follow-up perceptual study in which the choice was not framed in terms of 'accept' or 'reject' but using a different kind of instruction (i.e. 'choose the option with fewer or more dots') suggests that attention acts on a more fundamental mechanism of information processing that goes beyond simple Pavlovian influences.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results across the two experiments.

claims.claim: Confidence is influenced by the perceived sense of uncertainty in the evaluation process and contextual cues.
claims.source: We found that the role of confidence goes beyond that of simply tracking the probability of an action being correct, as proposed in standard signal detection theory. Instead, it is also influenced by the perceived sense of uncertainty in the evaluation process (Navajas et al., 2017; Vaghi et al., 2017), and contextual cues (Lebreton et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings and citations to related work.

claims.claim: Confidence influences future responses and information seeking.
claims.source: In turn, confidence influences future responses and information seeking (Folke et al., 2017; Guggenmos et al., 2016; Fleming et al., 2018; Rollwage et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The sense of confidence is shaped by the behavioural goal that participants are set to achieve.
claims.source: This suggests that similarly to attention, the sense of confidence is also shaped by the behavioural goal that participants are set to achieve.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about confidence.

claims.claim: The incorporation of goal-relevant evidence to fit the GLAM resulted in a better model fit compared with the model in which the value or perceptual evidence was integrated independently of the frame.
claims.source: In both experiments, the incorporation of goal-relevant evidence to fit the GLAM resulted in a better model fit compared with the model in which the value or perceptual evidence was integrated independently of the frame.
claims.evidence: This is supported by model comparison analysis.

claims.claim: The empirical confidence data provide support to a multiplicative instead of additive effect of attention into goal-relevant information.
claims.source: Our empirical confidence data therefore provide further support to a multiplicative (Smith and Krajbich, 2019) instead of additive effect of attention into goal-relevant information.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results and experimental data.

claims.claim: The goal sets, from the beginning of the task, the allocation of attention and influences first-order processes such as choice, but also second order process such as confidence.
claims.source: Overall, these data speak in favour of a coding scheme in which the goal sets, from the beginning of the task, the allocation of attention and, by doing so, influences first-order processes such as choice, but also second order process such as confidence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claims.claim: There has been surprisingly little experimental work in which the behavioural goal has been directly manipulated as the key experimental variable for studying the relation between attention and value.
claims.source: Nevertheless, there has been a surprisingly little amount of experimental work in which the behavioural goal has been directly manipulated as the key experimental variable for studying the relation between attention and value.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the field.

claims.claim: Frömer et al., 2019 found that behaviour and neural activity in the 'value network' was determined by goal-congruency and did not simply reflected the expected reward.
claims.source: In the first study (Frömer et al., 2019), participants were shown a set of four items and asked, in half of the trials, to determine the best item and, in the second half, the worst item. In line with our findings, they found that behaviour and neural activity in the 'value network', including vmPFC and striatum, was determined by goal-congruency and did not simply reflected the expected reward.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claims.claim: Kovach et al., 2014 found that the overall pattern of attention was mostly allocated according to the task goal.
claims.source: In the second study, Kovach et al., 2014 implemented a design similar to our value-based experiment in which participants were required to indicate the item to keep and the one to discard. They found, similarly to our findings in the value-based experiment, that the overall pattern of attention was mostly allocated according to the task goal.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claims.claim: Kovach et al., 2014 found that in the first few hundred milliseconds, attention was directed more prominently to the most valuable item in both conditions.
claims.source: However, in the first few hundred milliseconds, these authors found that attention was directed more prominently to the most valuable item in both conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claims.claim: The current study did not replicate the finding that fixations were directed to the most valuable item in the early moments of the trial.
claims.source: We did not replicate this last finding in our experiment (see Figure 3C and D and Appendix 2—figure 2, showing that fixations were randomly allocated during the early moments of the trial).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D and Appendix 2—figure 2.

claims.claim: The gaze-contingent presentation in the current study might have prevented an initial bottom-up attention grab from the most valuable item.
claims.source: One possible reason for this discrepancy is that the experiment by Kovach and colleagues presented both items on the screen at the beginning of the task – unlike in our task, in which the item was presented in a gaze-contingent way (to avoid processing in the visual periphery). This setting might have triggered an initial and transitory bottom-up attention grab from the most valuable (and often most salient) item before the accumulation process started.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference between studies.

claims.claim: When the agent needs to select the best item in a set, it is best to search for evidence that it is more likely to affect the top of the ranking.
claims.source: When the agent needs to select the best item in a set, it is best to search for evidence that it is more likely to affect the top of the ranking (e.g. is the best item still the best one?); information that changes the middle or the bottom of the ranking is instead less valuable (e.g. is the item ranked as seven is now ranked as six?) because it would not affect the behavioural output.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claims.claim: When choosing which item to discard, the optimal strategy involves acquiring information most informative of the bottom of the ranking and not the top.
claims.source: When choosing which item to discard, instead, the optimal strategy involves acquiring information most informative of the bottom of the ranking and not the top.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the economic model.

claims.claim: Context and behavioural demand have a powerful effect on how information is accumulated and processed.
claims.source: The most far reaching conclusion of our work is that context and behavioural demand have a powerful effect on how information is accumulated and processed.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: This is a general effect that spans both more complex value-based choice and simpler perceptual choice.
claims.source: Notably, our data show that this is a general effect that spans both more complex value-based choice and simpler perceptual choice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing results across the two experiments.

claims.claim: Humans have developed a mechanism that prioritises the processing or recollection of the information that is most relevant for the behavioural response that is required.
claims.source: Our conclusion is that, given the limited computational resources of the brain, humans have developed a mechanism that prioritises the processing or recollection of the information that is most relevant for the behavioural response that is required.
claims.evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: From the very beginning of the deliberation process, the context affects which information is processed, recalled, or attended to, with effects that spread into post-decision processing such as confidence estimation.
claims.source: As we have shown here, from the very beginning of the deliberation process, the context — even when it is simple (like/dislike, most/fewest) or irrelevant from the experimenter perspective — affects which information is processed, recalled, or attended to, with effects that spread into post-decision processing such as confidence estimation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Many of the so-called 'biases' might be shown in a new light, given that participants are dealing with very different choices once the behavioural goal changes.
claims.source: With this shift of perspective, it may well be the case that many of the so-called 'biases' will be shown in a new light, given that participants are dealing with very different choices once the behavioural goal changes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings.

claims.claim: Evolution has equipped humans well to deal with ever-changing environments in the face of limited computational resources.
claims.source: This viewpoint might provide a more encouraging picture of the human mind, by suggesting that evolution has equipped us well to deal with ever-changing environments in the face of limited computational resources.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Participants were asked to fast for 4 hr previous to the experiment, expecting they would be hungry and willing to spend money to buy a snack.
claims.source: Participants were asked to fast for 4 hr previous to the experiment, expecting they would be hungry and willing to spend money to buy a snack.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experiment.

claims.claim: Pairs were selected using the value ratings given in the bidding task: using a median split, each item was categorised as high- or low-value for the agent.
claims.source: Pairs were selected using the value ratings given in the bidding task: using a median split, each item was categorised as high- or low-value for the agent; these were then combined to produce 15 high-value, 15 low-value, and 30 mixed pairs, for a total of 60 pairs tailored to the participant's preferences.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experiment.

claims.claim: Participants' eye movements were recorded throughout the choice task and the presentation of food items was gaze-contingent.
claims.source: Participants' eye movements were recorded throughout the choice task and the presentation of food items was gaze-contingent: participants could only see one item at a time depending on which box they looked at; following Folke et al., 2017, this was done to reduce the risk that participant, while gazing one item, would still look at the other item in their visual periphery.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological detail of the experiment.

claims.claim: Forty volunteers gave their informed consent to take part in the Value Experiment research.
claims.source: Forty volunteers gave their informed consent to take part in this research.
claims.evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the study.

claims.claim: Thirty-one participants passed the exclusion criteria and were included in the analysis of the Value Experiment.
claims.source: Of these, 31 passed the exclusion criteria and were included in the analysis (16 females, 17 males, aged 20–54, mean age of 28.8).
claims.evidence: This describes the final sample for the Value Experiment.

claims.claim: Forty volunteers were recruited for the Perceptual Experiment.
claims.source: Forty volunteers were recruited for the second experiment.
claims.evidence: This describes the participant recruitment for the Perceptual Experiment.

claims.claim: Thirty-two participants were included in the behavioural and regression analyses of the Perceptual Experiment.
claims.source: Thirty-two participants (22 females, 10 males, aged 19–50, mean age of 26.03) were included in the behavioural and regression analyses.
claims.evidence: This describes the final sample for the Perceptual Experiment.

claims.claim: The optimal strategy when choosing the best option is to acquire one more signal about item i1 or i2.
claims.source: Proposition 1. The optimal strategy when choosing the best option is to acquire one more signal about item i1 or i2, that is, either the item with the currently highest expected value or the one with second highest value.
claims.evidence: This is a formal proposition from the economic model.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the prevailing view in the field: that visual attention increases value, people look longer at higher-value options, and choose options they attend to more. This interpretation assumes attention operates over value itself.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C5-C7, and C10 consistently describe established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations to prior work. These claims accurately characterize the dominant theoretical framework the study aims to challenge.

results.result: Recent studies have begun questioning whether attention operates purely over value, suggesting attention may have a flexible role in sampling goal-relevant options and that 'value networks' may track goal-congruent information rather than pure reward value.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by citations to recent research (Kovach et al., 2014; Glickman et al., 2018; Frömer et al., 2019; Suri et al., 2020) that challenges the dominant view, providing context for the current study's hypothesis.

results.result: The main finding: attention does not boost value per se, but instead modulates goal-relevant information. In value-based tasks, participants looked longer at the item they selected (high-value in 'like' frame, low-value in 'dislike' frame), not necessarily the most valuable item. This pattern generalizes across both value-based and perceptual decision tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C13-C15, C18-C21, C77-C78 present converging evidence from experimental data with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests, hierarchical logistic regression) showing significant effects (p<0.001) in predicted directions. The replication across two independent experiments (value-based and perceptual) with different participant groups strengthens the conclusion. ΔDT positively predicted choice in both frames, supporting goal-relevance over pure value.

results.result: Participants understood the task manipulations and made appropriate choices: selecting higher-value items in 'like' frame and lower-value items in 'dislike' frame, with choice accuracy modulated by confidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 1B,C) and replicate previous findings (De Martino et al., 2013; Folke et al., 2017). This validates that the experimental manipulation was effective and participants complied with instructions.

results.result: The magnitude of the ΔDT effect on choice showed small but significant differences between frames: slightly lower in dislike vs. like frame (Value Experiment), but higher in fewest vs. most frame (Perceptual Experiment).
results.evaluation: Claims C22 and C25 report statistically significant differences (p<0.05) with appropriate tests. However, the opposite pattern between experiments suggests these may be minor modulations rather than fundamental differences in the underlying mechanism.

results.result: In the Perceptual Experiment, participants' gaze was preferentially allocated to the goal-relevant option: more time observing circles with more dots in 'most' frame and fewer dots in 'fewest' frame. ΔDT positively predicted choice in both frames.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by strong statistical evidence (t(31)=13.85, p<0.001 for most; t(31)=-10.88, p<0.001 for fewest; z>10, p<0.001 for ΔDT effects). This replicates the value-based findings in a perceptual domain, strengthening generalizability.

results.result: The last fixation effect, a key prediction of attentional accumulation models, was replicated but showed goal-dependent modulation: in 'like'/'most' frames, probability of choosing the last-fixated item increased with its value/evidence, but this reversed in 'dislike'/'fewest' frames.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C32 show the last fixation effect with strong statistical support (mean β coefficients with significant frame differences: t(30)=7.963, p<0.001 for Value; t(31)=3.727, p<0.001 for Perceptual). The reversal pattern is consistent with goal-relevant processing rather than pure value accumulation.

results.result: Goal-relevant attention allocation persists throughout trials, not just in the final fixation. After removing the last two fixations, the ΔDT pattern remained unchanged. Middle fixation durations and time-series analysis showed goal-relevant modulation throughout the trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 address a critical alternative explanation (that effects are driven solely by last fixation). The supplementary analyses (Appendix 2-figure 3, Figure 3C) and replication of middle fixation effects from prior studies provide converging evidence that goal-relevance operates throughout the decision process.

results.result: In the Value Experiment, confidence was influenced by |ΔValue|, RT, and GSF as expected, but critically, the effect of ΣValue on confidence reversed between frames: positive in 'like' frame (higher confidence when both items high-value) but negative in 'dislike' frame (higher confidence when both items low-value).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C42 present hierarchical linear regression results with strong statistical support (z-scores >5, p<0.001 for main effects; t(30)=9.91, p<0.001 for frame difference in ΣValue effect). The reversal of ΣValue effect is a novel finding suggesting confidence also tracks goal-relevant information. The replication of known effects (C37-C39) validates the analysis approach.

results.result: In the Perceptual Experiment, confidence showed parallel patterns to the Value Experiment: influenced by |ΔDots|, RT, and GSF, with a critical reversal in the effect of ΣDots between 'most' (positive) and 'fewest' (negative) frames.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 replicate the confidence findings from the Value Experiment in a perceptual domain with strong statistical support (z-scores >3, p<0.001; t(31)=14.621, p<0.001 for frame difference). This cross-domain replication strengthens the conclusion that confidence tracks goal-relevant information generally.

results.result: The Gaze-weighted Linear Accumulator Model (GLAM) was adapted to test the goal-relevant evidence hypothesis by using goal-relevant evidence (not raw value/dots) as input for 'dislike'/'fewest' frames. This approach provided better model fit than models using frame-independent evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 and C84 describe the modeling approach with appropriate justification (GLAM allows balance-of-evidence confidence measures unlike aDDM). The claim of better fit (C84) is supported by model comparison (referenced in appendices). This is a critical methodological choice that operationalizes the goal-relevance hypothesis.

results.result: In the Value Experiment, GLAM simulations successfully predicted out-of-sample behavioral patterns: RT decreased with |ΔValue| (r=0.89-0.90, p<0.001), choice probability patterns in both frames (r=0.79-0.80, p<0.001), and gaze influence on choice (r=0.63-0.68, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C57 demonstrate strong model validation with high correlations between predicted and observed behavior on held-out data (odd-numbered trials). The model captures the frame-dependent reversal in choice patterns (C54), supporting the goal-relevant evidence framework. Parameters were fit on even trials and tested on odd trials, providing appropriate cross-validation.

results.result: In the Perceptual Experiment, GLAM replicated RT patterns (r=0.97-0.98, p<0.001) and gaze influence (r=0.47-0.65, p<0.05), but choice predictions were significant only for 'fewest' frame (r=0.37, p=0.051 for 'most'; r=0.69, p<0.001 for 'fewest').
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 show mixed results. While RT and gaze influence predictions are strong, the choice prediction in 'most' frame is marginal (p=0.051). This asymmetry between frames in the Perceptual Experiment is not fully explained and suggests potential limitations in model fit or task-specific factors. The weaker performance compared to the Value Experiment warrants further investigation.

results.result: Models fitted without accounting for goal-relevant evidence provided poor fit. Both GLAM and aDDM showed that models using goal-relevant evidence fit better than those using frame-independent evidence for 'dislike'/'fewest' frames.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by model comparison analyses presented in appendices (Appendix 5, Appendix 7). The convergence of results across two different modeling frameworks (GLAM and aDDM) strengthens the conclusion that goal-relevant evidence is necessary to explain the data.

results.result: GLAM simulations using balance of evidence (Δe) as a confidence proxy replicated the empirical ΣValue/ΣDots effects on confidence, but only when gaze bias was included in the model. This suggests the multiplicative effect of attention on evidence accumulation generates the confidence patterns, supporting a multiplicative rather than additive attentional effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C71 and C85 present a mechanistic account linking attention, evidence accumulation, and confidence. The critical finding that ΣValue/ΣDots effects disappear without gaze bias (C67, C69) is well-supported statistically (effects become non-significant when bias removed). This provides computational support for the multiplicative attention hypothesis and explains the novel confidence findings. However, C71 acknowledges this is somewhat speculative about the precise mechanism.

results.result: An economic model of optimal information acquisition shows that when choosing the best item from n>2 options, it's optimal to acquire information about top-ranked items; when choosing which to discard, it's optimal to acquire information about bottom-ranked items. For binary choice (n=2), agents are indifferent.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76, C93-C94, and C108 present formal propositions from an economic model with proofs in Appendix 9. The mathematical reasoning is sound: information is most valuable when it affects the behavioral output. This provides a normative framework suggesting the observed asymmetric attention strategies may reflect optimal behavior generalized from multi-alternative contexts to binary choice.

results.result: The overarching conclusion: context and behavioral goals powerfully affect information accumulation and processing from the start of deliberation, extending to post-decision processes like confidence. This is a general effect spanning value-based and perceptual choice, reflecting an adaptive mechanism for prioritizing goal-relevant information given limited computational resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 and C95-C98 synthesize the empirical findings into broader conclusions. The support comes from converging evidence across two experiments, multiple dependent measures (gaze, choice, RT, confidence), time-series analyses showing early effects (C79), and replication in perceptual domain ruling out Pavlovian explanations (C80). The conclusions are well-justified by the data presented.

results.result: Confidence is shaped by behavioral goals, going beyond tracking choice accuracy to reflect perceived uncertainty and contextual factors. The goal influences both first-order processes (choice) and second-order processes (confidence) from the beginning of the task through attentional allocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 and C86 are supported by the novel confidence findings (ΣValue/ΣDots reversal) and citations to related work. The inference that goals shape confidence through attention (C86) is supported by the modeling results showing gaze bias is necessary to reproduce confidence patterns. This extends prior understanding of confidence beyond simple accuracy tracking.

results.result: The study relates to limited prior work directly manipulating behavioral goals. Frömer et al. (2019) found goal-congruent neural activity; Kovach et al. (2014) found goal-dependent attention but with early bias toward high-value items. The current study did not replicate this early bias, possibly due to gaze-contingent presentation preventing bottom-up capture.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 accurately characterize prior work (C88-C90 supported by citations) and note a discrepancy with Kovach et al. regarding early fixations (C91 supported by Figure 3C,D and Appendix 2-figure 2). The proposed explanation (C92) is speculative but reasonable given methodological differences. This contextualizes the current findings appropriately.

results.result: The findings suggest many 'biases' in decision-making may reflect adaptive processing given that behavioral goals fundamentally change the decision problem. This provides an optimistic view of human cognition as well-adapted to changing environments despite limited resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are speculative interpretations extending beyond the data. While the findings do show goal-dependent processing, the leap to reinterpreting 'biases' broadly and evolutionary claims about adaptation requires additional evidence. These are interesting implications but remain hypothetical.

results.result: Methodological details: Value Experiment used 31 participants (from 40 recruited) who fasted 4hr, made choices between snack pairs selected via median-split of BDM bids, with gaze-contingent presentation. Perceptual Experiment used 32 participants (from 40 recruited) with similar gaze-contingent design.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C107 describe methodological details that are clearly stated and appropriate. Sample sizes (n=31, n=32) are reasonable for within-subject designs with multiple trials. Exclusion criteria are specified. The gaze-contingent design is justified to prevent peripheral processing. BDM mechanism is incentive-compatible for value elicitation.
